title: Nearest Matching Word on a Ring
statement:
The strings in words are arranged in a ring: after the last word comes the first one again, and before the first comes the last. You stand at index start. One step moves you to the neighbouring word on the left or on the right.

Return the fewest steps needed to stand on a word equal to target. If target is not in words, return -1.

examples.why: Walking right takes 3 steps. Walking left wraps around: 1 → 0 → 4 is only 2.
You are already on a matching word.

hints: For one matching index i, what are the two possible walking distances from start?
Going one way costs |i − start| steps; going the other way around costs n − |i − start|. Take the smaller.
Take the minimum of that over every matching index. Or walk outward from start in both directions at once and stop at the first match.

explain.intuition:
On a ring there are exactly two routes between two positions: the direct one, of length d = |i − start|, and the one that wraps around the end, of length n − d. The shorter is min(d, n − d).

So check every index that holds target and keep the smallest such distance. An equivalent way that can stop early: step outward with two pointers, one going left and one going right (both wrapping with modulo), and return the step count as soon as either lands on target. After n / 2 steps both have covered the whole ring.
steps: For each i with words[i] === target, let d = |i − start| and update best with min(d, n − d).
pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around route, so the first example gives 3 instead of 2.
Computing the left index as (start − k) % n in JavaScript, which goes negative. Use (start − k + n) % n.
Returning the index of the match instead of the number of steps.

solutions.title: Distance to every match
solutions.idea: For each matching index, the ring distance is min(d, n − d) with d = |i − start|.

solutions.title: Expand outward in both directions
solutions.idea: Two pointers walk left and right from start, wrapping around; the first one to hit target gives the answer.

followups: Answer many queries (target, start) on the same ring. What would you precompute?
Moving left costs 2 per step and moving right costs 1. What changes?
lcTitle: Shortest Distance to Target String in a Circular Array
